Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

vignette:
David is a 52-year-old school principal who came to treatment at his wife's urging after months of telling himself that what happened should have been behind him by now. The assault occurred late one evening at school after a winter sports event. Most of the building had emptied out, and he was making a final round through the hallways before locking up. He remembered stepping into a side corridor near the gym where the lights were dimmer and hearing movement behind him before he could place it. A man came at him suddenly, close and fast. What stayed with David most vividly was not a coherent sequence he could easily retell, but flashes: the shock of being grabbed, the hard angle of his body forced awkwardly against the wall and then down, the helpless awareness of nearby objects that could be used to hurt him, and the sensation of being trapped in a position where he could not orient himself or get away. Even in session, when he tried to explain exactly how it unfolded, he would falter and say that when he deliberately reached for the memory, it seemed to recede or break apart. Yet at other times the scene returned with punishing clarity, like a film already loaded and running.

In the weeks afterward, David returned to work because he felt he had to. As principal, he was used to being the one who kept order, reassured others, and knew what to do in a crisis. He found it difficult to tolerate how often his body now reacted before his mind caught up. Walking into faculty meetings, parent conferences, assemblies, or even a classroom observation, he automatically located the exits before he could focus on who was speaking. If a custodian had left a heavy flashlight on a counter, if a letter opener sat on a secretary's desk, if sports equipment was stacked in a corner, his attention snagged on it immediately. He was not thinking in any abstract way about danger; he simply noticed, instantly, what in the room could become a weapon. He described it as his eyes doing their own work.

The school environment gave him constant occasions for this. At the front entrance during morning arrival, a dropped metal thermos or the slam of a locker could make him jolt so sharply that nearby students looked at him. During security drills, which had once felt procedural, he became acutely aware of every doorway and blind corner. In the auditorium, he chose seats at the edge. During staff development days in unfamiliar district buildings, he entered each room already scanning how he would get out. He was embarrassed by this, particularly because he was meant to project calm. He had come to believe that letting his attention drift, even briefly, was unsafe.

His memory of the assault remained oddly divided. If asked by police, his wife, or later by himself in the quiet of night, he found it hard to call up a complete, deliberate account. He could not reliably put the moments in order or explain certain stretches of time. That frustrated him, and he worried about what it meant that he could not simply narrate the event from beginning to end. But the memory also arrived uninvited with a force that made the uncertainty irrelevant. He would be sitting at his desk reviewing budgets, or standing in the hallway while students changed classes, and suddenly the scene would replay as if projected in front of him. At those moments he did not feel like a man remembering something from months ago. His body seemed to drop back into the same posture from the assault: shoulders tightened, torso braced, neck fixed at an angle, as though he were again pinned and waiting for the next blow. He sometimes realized only afterward that he had been holding himself rigidly in his chair or gripping the edge of his desk.

At home, his wife noticed that restaurants became complicated because he insisted on facing the door and grew tense in crowded rooms. He did not offer much explanation beyond saying he liked to know where the exits were. Over time, the strain showed in quieter ways. He stayed later in his office to avoid entering bustling spaces with other adults, then came home irritable and exhausted. He avoided school social events held off campus because unfamiliar venues made him feel immediately on guard. His wife saw how often his attention moved around a room instead of resting on her, and David felt ashamed that he could not seem to stop.

What finally brought him in was a recent incident at school when a stack of folding chairs crashed in the cafeteria. He lurched violently at the sound, and for a split second the assault was there again in full motion, his body already set into that same trapped position before he knew where he was. Several students stared. Later, alone in his office, he found that when he tried to calmly think through the original assault, the details still would not come in a steady way. He sought help because he was frightened by both sides of this experience: that the memory could seize him so completely, and that when he tried to reach for it on purpose, it remained out of grasp. More than anything, he hopes to feel present again in the school he has led for years, and he is afraid that if this continues, every room he enters will keep feeling like a place he first has to survive.
